claims.text: Formation of a uniform, single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticle under rapid heating and cooling is governed by heterogeneous-nucleation kinetics.
Pre-formed, compatible single-phase alloy seeds promote epitaxial nucleation.
Seeding lowers the nucleation or crystallization energy barrier.
Seed-mediated nucleation suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation.
Au-Pd alloy seeds can provide a known FCC template for an Au-Pd-Rh-Ir-Ru target system.
Rapid thermal processing under inert or reducing conditions is applicable to forming single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Matching the seed lattice parameters to the anticipated HEA structure enables coherent epitaxial growth.
The coherent seed lattice directs deposition and alloying of incoming metal atoms.
Epitaxial templating by FCC seeds promotes uniform FCC phase formation during the rapid thermal cycle.
Relative to unseeded synthesis, seeded synthesis will consistently yield a more uniform single-phase FCC structure.
Relative to unseeded synthesis, seeded synthesis will improve compositional homogeneity.
Relative to unseeded synthesis, seeded synthesis will provide more controlled particle morphology.
Heating parameters may need adjustment to prevent sintering.
In the unseeded rapid-heating and cooling baseline, uncontrolled nucleation causes phase separation, elemental segregation, and variable crystal structure.
The proposed effect is expected only when the seed is sufficiently lattice-matched to the target HEA.
Significant seed-to-product lattice mismatch can disrupt the proposed structural control.
Excessive heating duration can promote unwanted grain growth.
Rapid heating and rapid cooling can preserve a single solid solution by suppressing secondary-phase formation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis invokes heterogeneous, seed-mediated epitaxial nucleation but says that seeds lower the barrier for 'homogeneous crystallization.' Seed-mediated nucleation is heterogeneous, so the stated nucleation classifications conflict.
